title: Storage & File Organization
summary: Where data actually lives — from CPU registers to spinning disks — and how DBMSs pack it into pages, files, and RAID arrays to make queries fast.

blocks.markdown:
A DBMS keeps data on **persistent storage** (disk or SSD) because RAM vanishes on power-off. Everything a database does to make queries fast — pages, indexes, RAID — is ultimately about hiding the enormous gap between disk speed and CPU speed.

- **Page/block**: the atomic unit of I/O; a DBMS reads one full page even if it wants one row.
- **File organization**: how records are arranged in pages on disk.
- **RAID**: how disks are combined for speed and fault-tolerance.

Memory gets slower, cheaper, and larger as you move down the hierarchy.

A CPU register access: ~0.3 ns. A hard-disk seek: ~8 ms. That is a **25 000× gap**.

blocks.subTitle: Volatile vs non-volatile
blocks.markdown:
**Volatile** storage (registers, cache, RAM) loses data when power is cut. **Non-volatile** (SSD, HDD, tape) persists.

- A database's **source of truth is always on non-volatile storage** — RAM is just a fast working space.
- **Buffer pool**: the region of RAM a DBMS manages as a cache for disk pages. Dirty pages must be flushed to disk before the buffer slot is reused.
- SSDs have no moving parts; HDDs use spinning platters + a read/write head that must seek.

For decades, **disk I/O was the database bottleneck**. Three sources of HDD latency:

- **Seek time** — arm moves to the right track (~4–8 ms).
- **Rotational latency** — disk spins to the right sector (~2–4 ms at 7 200 RPM).
- **Transfer time** — data moves off the platter (small).

SSDs eliminate seek and rotation, cutting random read latency to ~0.1 ms — but disk-era design decisions (pages, buffer pools, sequential I/O preference) are baked into every major DBMS. See [query-processing-optimization](query-processing-optimization).

blocks.subTitle: What and why
blocks.markdown:
**RAID** (Redundant Array of Independent Disks) combines multiple physical disks into one logical volume. Goals:

- **Performance** — read/write in parallel across multiple disks.
- **Fault-tolerance** — survive one (or more) disk failures without data loss.
- **Striping**: data is split across disks in chunks — sequential reads become parallel.
- **Mirroring**: the same data is written to two disks — any one can fail without loss.
- **Parity**: a computed check value that lets you reconstruct a failed disk's data from the others.

blocks.subTitle: Level trade-offs
blocks.markdown:
Common RAID levels and their profiles.

| Level | Technique | Fault-tolerance |
|---|---|---|
| RAID 0 | Striping only | None (1 failure = total loss) |
| RAID 1 | Mirroring | 1 disk failure |
| RAID 5 | Striping + distributed parity | 1 disk failure |
| RAID 6 | Striping + dual parity | 2 disk failures |
| RAID 10 | Mirror + stripe | 1 per mirrored pair |

**RAID 5** is the most common production choice — good storage efficiency + fault-tolerance. **RAID 10** costs double the space but rebuilds instantly (no parity math).

blocks.subTitle: The unit of I/O
blocks.markdown:
A **record** is one row of a table, stored as a sequence of field values on disk.

- A **block** (or **page**) is the fixed-size chunk the OS/disk hardware reads and writes atomically — typically **4 KB or 8 KB** (Postgres default: 8 KB).
- A DBMS **always reads an entire page** even if only one row is needed. This is why fetching a single row by primary key is fast only with an index — otherwise every page must be checked.
- **Fixed-length records** are simple: fields always at the same byte offset. **Variable-length records** (VARCHAR, TEXT) need a header or slot-array to find each field.

blocks.subTitle: Blocking factor
blocks.markdown:
**Blocking factor** (BF) = how many records fit in one block.

`BF = floor(block_size / record_size)`

Example: 8 KB block, 200-byte record → BF = floor(8192 / 200) = **40 records/block**.

- A table with 1 000 000 records needs ceil(1 000 000 / 40) = **25 000 blocks** on disk.
- A full table scan reads all 25 000 blocks — the bigger BF, the fewer I/Os. Narrow records pack tighter and scan faster.

blocks.subTitle: Heap (unordered)
blocks.markdown:
A **heap file** (also called an unordered file) appends new records wherever there is free space — no ordering is maintained.

- **Insert**: O(1) — write to the last page.
- **Search**: O(N) — must scan every block (linear search).
- **Delete**: marks record as deleted; space is reclaimed lazily.
- Best for: bulk loading, append-heavy workloads, tables that are always scanned in full (e.g. log tables).
- Worst for: point queries on large tables — without an index every page must be read.

blocks.subTitle: Sequential (sorted)
blocks.markdown:
A **sequential file** keeps records physically sorted by an **ordering field** (e.g., employee ID).

- **Search on ordering field**: O(log N) blocks — binary search possible.
- **Insert**: expensive — must find the right position and shift records; often handled via an overflow chain.
- **Range queries**: very fast — once the start is found, records are contiguous.
- Used as the basis for **dense/sparse indexes**. See [indexing](indexing).

blocks.subTitle: Hash
blocks.markdown:
A **hash file** applies a hash function to the search key to compute the target **bucket** (page or group of pages) directly.

- **Point query**: ~O(1) — hash maps straight to the bucket.
- **Range queries**: useless — hashing destroys order.
- **Overflow buckets** handle collisions when a bucket fills up.
- Static hashing (fixed bucket count) struggles as the file grows; **extendible hashing** doubles the bucket directory dynamically.

blocks.subTitle: Clustered & heap vs sorted vs hash
blocks.markdown:
A **clustered file** co-locates records from related tables in the same pages — useful when two tables are almost always joined.

Summary of file organizations:

| Organization | Point query | Range query |
|---|---|---|
| Heap | O(N) — full scan | O(N) — full scan |
| Sequential | O(log N) — binary | O(log N) — contiguous |
| Hash | O(1) — bucket | Poor — order lost |

No single organization wins all workloads — DBMSs use **indexes** on top of heap/sequential files to compensate. See [indexing](indexing).

**ISAM** (Indexed Sequential Access Method) layers a static index tree on top of a sequential file.

- The data file is sorted; a separate **index file** holds (key, block pointer) pairs.
- **Search**: follow the index to the right block, then scan within it — fast.
- **Insert**: if target block is full, records spill into a chained **overflow page**.
- **Problem**: heavy inserts degrade into long overflow chains, making later reads slow. Long-term, the tree must be rebuilt.
- ISAM was surpassed by **B+ trees** (dynamic, self-balancing). See [indexing](indexing).

Common misconceptions:

- **"SSD made disk design irrelevant."** No — pages, buffer pools, and sequential-I/O preference all still matter on SSDs; random writes still cost more than sequential.
- **"RAID replaces backups."** RAID survives disk failure but not accidental deletes, corruption, or site disasters — backups are separate.
- **"Hash files work for range queries."** A hash function destroys sort order; hash files are useless for `BETWEEN` or `ORDER BY`.
- **"A bigger block is always better."** Large blocks waste I/O if queries only touch one small record per page (low selectivity).

blocks.subTitle: Why read whole pages?
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: Why does a database read an entire page even when it only wants one row?**

Disk hardware (and the OS) transfers data in fixed-size blocks — there is no mechanism to read just one record's bytes without pulling the whole block. The DBMS exploits this: once a page is in the buffer pool, all records on it are available cheaply. This is also why a full table scan isn't as catastrophic as it sounds — it reads pages sequentially, which is the fastest disk access pattern.

blocks.subTitle: RAID 5 vs RAID 10
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: RAID 5 vs RAID 10 — when would you choose each for a database?**

**RAID 5**: efficient storage (only 1 disk overhead), tolerates 1 failure, but writes are slow (must compute and update parity) and rebuild after failure takes hours — during which a second failure kills everything.

**RAID 10**: mirrors every disk (50% space overhead), extremely fast writes (no parity), and rebuilds in minutes. Choose RAID 10 for write-heavy databases where rebuild time and write latency matter more than raw storage cost.

blocks.subTitle: Heap vs clustered file
blocks.markdown:
**Q: When would you use a heap file vs a clustered file organization?**

**Heap**: best for bulk-loaded data, append-only logs, or tables that are always fully scanned — no overhead maintaining order.

**Clustered**: best when two tables are almost always joined together — placing their rows in shared pages eliminates I/O on every join. Cost: inserts into a clustered file are more complex. Most real DBMSs (e.g. InnoDB) cluster the primary table on the primary key by default.

blocks.subTitle: What is blocking factor?
blocks.markdown:
**Q: What is blocking factor and why does it affect query performance?**

**Blocking factor** (BF) = records per block = `floor(block_size / record_size)`.

A higher BF means fewer blocks to read for a full table scan — directly fewer I/Os. Wider records (many columns, large text fields) reduce BF. This is one reason SELECT * is discouraged on large tables: it forces wide records into the buffer pool even when only a few columns are needed.

blocks.subTitle: Hash file limitations
blocks.markdown:
**Q: Why can't a hash file organization support range queries efficiently?**

A hash function maps a key to a bucket pseudo-randomly — records with adjacent keys land in unrelated buckets. There is no way to locate all records where key is between X and Y without scanning every bucket. For range queries, a **sorted sequential file** or a **B+ tree index** is needed. See [indexing](indexing).

blocks.subTitle: ISAM vs B+ tree
blocks.markdown:
**Q: Why did ISAM lose to B+ trees?**

ISAM's index is **static** — inserted records that don't fit in a block chain into overflow pages. After heavy inserts, searches must follow long overflow chains, destroying the O(log N) guarantee. B+ trees are **dynamic**: the tree rebalances on every insert, so search depth stays logarithmic regardless of insert pattern. ISAM only makes sense on read-mostly, rarely-updated datasets.

Storage organization underpins everything above it.

- **Indexing** builds on file organizations — a B+ tree index on a heap file gives point and range queries without restructuring the data file. See [indexing](indexing).
- **Query processing** counts I/Os using block reads; every join algorithm (nested loop, hash join, merge join) is analyzed in blocks. See [query-processing-optimization](query-processing-optimization).
- **Recovery** writes to disk pages; WAL (write-ahead logging) is a sequential file. See [recovery-systems](recovery-systems).
